title: Headers and Multi-file Programs
summary: Split a program into source files and headers, protect headers with include guards, control visibility with static and extern, and automate the build with a Makefile.
introduction: Every real C program is more than one file. Each `.c` file is compiled separately into an object file and the linker joins them; headers are how one file learns the names that another defines. Done right, this gives fast incremental builds and clean module boundaries. Done wrong, it gives duplicate-definition errors and headers that break when included twice. This lesson builds a small two-module program, explains declarations versus definitions, shows include guards, `static` and `extern`, and ends with a Makefile that rebuilds only what changed.
learningObjectives: Explain translation units and why a prototype must be visible in every file that calls a function
Write a header with an include guard and a matching source file
Use static and extern to control which names are shared between files
Write a minimal Makefile for a multi-file program

blocks.text: The compiler processes one **translation unit** at a time: a `.c` file plus everything its `#include` lines paste in. It never looks at other `.c` files, so to call a function defined elsewhere it needs a **declaration**, a prototype, in the current unit. A **definition** is the function body or the variable itself, and the *one definition rule* says each must exist exactly once across the whole program. Headers therefore hold declarations and are included wherever they are needed; definitions stay in `.c` files.
A header and its source file

The module below computes simple statistics. `stats.h` declares what the module offers; `stats.c` implements it; `main.c` uses it. `#include "stats.h"` with quotes searches the directory of the including file before the system directories, which `<...>` searches alone. Including the header in `stats.c` as well lets the compiler check that the definitions match their declarations.

blocks.title: stats.h
stats.c
main.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 -c stats.c
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 -c main.c
$ gcc stats.o main.o -o stats
$ ./stats
mean = 21.75
max  = 24.5

blocks.text: Each `-c` command produces one object file, and the final command links them. If you edit only `main.c`, only `main.o` needs rebuilding, which is what makes large projects compile in seconds. The shortcut `gcc stats.c main.c -o stats` does all three steps at once and is fine for small programs.

A header can be included more than once in a translation unit, directly or through another header. Declaring a function twice is harmless, but defining a struct or a typedef twice is an error. The **include guard** (`#ifndef NAME`, `#define NAME`, `#endif`) makes the preprocessor skip the body the second time. `#pragma once` does the same in every modern compiler and is shorter, but it is not part of the standard; guards work everywhere. Here is what the error looks like without a guard:

blocks.title: shape.h (no guard) and main.c
Terminal (trimmed)
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 main.c -o main
In file included from main.c:3:
shape.h:2:8: error: redefinition of 'struct shape'
    2 | struct shape { double w, h; };
      |        ^~~~~

blocks.text: By default every function and file-scope variable has **external linkage**: the linker can see its name, so other files may use it. Prefixing it with `static` gives it **internal linkage**: private to its file, and free to reuse the name elsewhere. A global variable shared between files is *defined* once in a `.c` file and *declared* in the header with `extern`, which says "this exists somewhere else". Shared globals make programs hard to reason about, so prefer passing values to functions and keep the few you need well named.

blocks.title: counter.h and counter.c
main.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 counter.c main.c -o calls
$ ./calls
call 1
call 2
total: 2

blocks.text: Typing three compiler commands after every edit does not scale. `make` reads a `Makefile` of rules in the form `target: prerequisites` followed by a recipe line that **must start with a tab**, and rebuilds a target only when a prerequisite is newer than it. Listing `stats.h` as a prerequisite ensures that editing the header recompiles every file that includes it.

blocks.title: Makefile
blocks.code:
CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 -g

stats: main.o stats.o
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) main.o stats.o -o stats

main.o: main.c stats.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c main.c

stats.o: stats.c stats.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c stats.c

clean:
	rm -f stats main.o stats.o

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.content:
$ make
gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 -g -c main.c
gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 -g -c stats.c
gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 -g main.o stats.o -o stats
$ make
make: 'stats' is up to date.

blocks.title: Common mistake: defining things in a header
blocks.text: A header that *defines* a variable (`int total_calls = 0;`) or contains a function body is pasted into every file that includes it, and the linker stops with `multiple definition of 'total_calls'`. Headers declare: prototypes, `extern` variables, struct and typedef definitions, macros. Definitions belong in exactly one `.c` file. The one exception is a small `static inline` function, which each file is allowed to have its own private copy of.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Add a `minimum` function to the stats module: declare it in `stats.h`, define it in `stats.c`, call it from `main.c`, then run `make` and watch which files are recompiled. Then touch only `main.c` and run `make` again.

questions.question: What is the difference between `#include <stats.h>` and `#include "stats.h"`?
questions.explanation: The quoted form searches the directory of the including file first and then falls back to the system directories; angle brackets search only the system directories. Use quotes for your own headers.
options: There is none; they are interchangeable
Quotes search the including file's directory first, then the system directories
Angle brackets are for C headers and quotes for C++ headers

questions.question: A function defined as `static` in one `.c` file can be called from another `.c` file as long as it is declared in a header.
questions.explanation: `static` gives the function internal linkage: its name is invisible to the linker outside its own file. A declaration elsewhere produces an undefined reference at link time.
